design_detail: Secondary analysis comparing two cohorts drawn from the pre-randomization phase of two residential research trials at one US research unit (Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, Baltimore): 103 adults with opioid dependence enrolled 2010 to 2015, before fentanyl reached the local supply and with urine positive for non-fentanyl opioids (Non-Fentanyl study), and 30 adults with opioid use disorder enrolled 2021 to February 2024 with fentanyl-positive urine (Fentanyl study). Both received the same fixed morphine stabilization for a week on the same unit, with withdrawal rated four times a day. The authors call it quasi-experimental; exposure was not assigned and the comparison group is historical.
can_establish: Whether, under one identical fixed morphine stabilization regimen in one residential unit, people entering with fentanyl exposure reported and showed more withdrawal symptoms, with a different day-by-day course, than people who entered a decade earlier with non-fentanyl opioid exposure.
cannot_establish: That fentanyl itself causes more severe withdrawal (the groups differ in era, parent trial, eligibility, age and concomitant medicines, and other adulterants such as xylazine or nitazenes could not be ruled out); the course of untreated withdrawal after stopping fentanyl (everyone was receiving morphine, so the outcome is withdrawal despite a fixed morphine regimen); effects beyond one week; how often severe withdrawal occurs outside research settings; or effect sizes (none are reported).

sample.recruitment: Adults with opioid use disorder recruited from the community into two randomized residential trials of opioid tapering at the same unit: tramadol extended-release against clonidine and buprenorphine (NCT01188421; October 2010 to June 2015) and a percutaneous nerve-stimulator device against lofexidine with placebo or sham (NCT04325659; enrolment from March 2021, ongoing; participants up to February 2024 included) (Methods › Parent Trials).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Non-Fentanyl trial: ages 18 to 60, DSM-IV opioid dependence, urine evidence of recent opioid use, no significant medical or psychiatric illness. Fentanyl trial: ages 22 to 65, DSM-5 opioid use disorder, urine evidence of recent opioid use, no significant medical or psychiatric illness. Both excluded pregnancy, physical dependence on alcohol or benzodiazepines needing withdrawal treatment, allergy to study medicines and current opioid agonist treatment. Full criteria in a supplementary table (not read).
sample.demographics: Combined: 56% Black or African American, 40% non-Hispanic White, 4% other; 84% men (Fentanyl study 76.7%, Non-Fentanyl 85.4%); 79% with at least high-school education. The Fentanyl group was older: mean age 46.0 (SD 10.1) against 41.2 (SD 10.2), p = 0.021; no other demographic difference was significant (Results › Participants; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not reported: the paper does not say how many participants contributed ratings on each stabilization day or whether anyone left during the stabilization week.
sample.selection_effects: Both cohorts volunteered for residential research trials of withdrawal management, which selects people willing to stop opioids under study conditions. The Fentanyl cohort is the first 30 of an ongoing trial. Different eras (about a decade apart), different diagnostic manuals and age limits, and urine confirmation of non-fentanyl status by chromatography in only 3 of 103 participants.

exposure.measurement: Urine at entry: all Fentanyl-study participants tested positive for fentanyl; all Non-Fentanyl participants tested positive on an opioid immunoassay with a morphine standard (which does not detect fentanyl), and the 3 tested by liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (all in the final study year) had no fentanyl or norfentanyl. Amount, frequency, route and duration of use and other drugs in the urine are not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study condition (the outcome period): immediate-release morphine 30 mg by subcutaneous injection four times a day for 7 days in both cohorts, on the same residential unit, before randomization in the parent trials. Withdrawal ratings and vital signs four times daily; analyses use each day's peak rating, days 1 to 7. In the Fentanyl trial only, protocolized concomitant medicines were available for withdrawal symptoms during stabilization (acetaminophen, antacid, clonazepam, dicyclomine, hydroxyzine, ibuprofen, loperamide, methocarbamol, milk of magnesia, ondansetron, promethazine, simethicone, trazodone), given after each data-collection time point.
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported. Both trials excluded physical dependence on alcohol or benzodiazepines needing withdrawal treatment. The authors note that xylazine had entered the local fentanyl supply and that nitazenes or other synthetic opioids may have been present; neither was measured.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants were in early abstinence from illicit opioids, receiving fixed morphine; time since last use at admission is not reported.

comparison.controls: Historical cohort: participants of the earlier trial with non-fentanyl opioid exposure, stabilized with the same morphine regimen on the same unit.
comparison.matching: None; no adjustment for age (the one demographic difference) or for era. Analyses are unadjusted two-way repeated-measures ANOVAs.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric comorbidity, pain, body mass index (which the authors link to fentanyl clearance), amount and duration of opioid use and other drug use were not compared between cohorts.

outcomes.instruments: Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scale (SOWS; 16 items, 0 to 64) and Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS; 11 items, 0 to 48) four times daily; severity categories for each; individual symptoms; heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, pupil diameter (pupillometer); tachycardia defined as heart rate above 100 beats a minute at least once.
outcomes.validity_norms: Both scales are standard published instruments. The SOWS categories are given as mild 1 to 10, moderate 11 to 20 and severe 21 to 30, which leaves scores above 30 on the 0 to 64 scale without a category.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcomes: each day's peak total SOWS and COWS score, and the percentage of participants in each severity category per day.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (alpha 0.05 throughout). The 35 counts the two total scores and their category analyses, 16 SOWS items, 11 COWS items, heart rate, two blood-pressure measures, pupil diameter and tachycardia, each with several model terms.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None. Self-ratings were made by participants who knew their own drug history; the authors state that COWS observers were not necessarily blind to fentanyl exposure.

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes, confidence intervals or between-group mean differences for the total scores are reported; daily means of total scores are in a supplementary table that was not read. Reported: SOWS model F(1,6) = 12.44, p < 0.01, with higher peak scores in the Fentanyl group on stabilization days 2 to 6 (text) or 2 to 5 (abstract); COWS model F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001, higher on days 2 to 7 (text) or 2 to 6 (abstract). Proportion rating severe self-reported withdrawal, Fentanyl against Non-Fentanyl: day 2, 48% against 16%; day 3, 47% against 8%; day 4, 37% against 6%; day 5, 27% against 6%. Observer-rated mild withdrawal: day 2, 73% against 33%; day 3, 70% against 13%; day 4, 73% against 18%; day 5, 60% against 15%; day 6, 53% against 18%; day 7, 40% against 14%; no one reached moderately severe or severe COWS scores. Tachycardia at least once 43% against 19%, p < 0.05. Heart rate study-by-time interaction p = 0.007; diastolic pressure interaction p = 0.022; smaller pupils in the Fentanyl group on all days (study effect p < 0.001).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Both parent trials are registered (NCT01188421, NCT04325659); this secondary comparison has no registered protocol or analysis plan.
analysis.selective_reporting: Many outcomes without correction. The abstract and the Results disagree about the days on which the groups differed, and one sentence attributes a study effect to systolic pressure inside the diastolic-pressure paragraph (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not addressed; the authors note the small Fentanyl group (30) may limit power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: On the same fixed morphine regimen, the 30 people who entered with fentanyl exposure rated their withdrawal higher than the 103 who entered with non-fentanyl opioids a decade earlier on most stabilization days after the first, with ratings that rose to a peak early in the week and then eased, while the earlier cohort's ratings fell steadily from the first day. Severe self-rated withdrawal was 3 to 6 times as common on days 2 to 5; observers rated most of the Fentanyl group as mildly withdrawn and almost none in either group above moderate. Tachycardia was more common (43% against 19%). Similar first-day ratings in both groups.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors call these data the first empirical demonstration that fentanyl exposure produces more severe and sustained withdrawal, and conclude that withdrawal remained elevated despite morphine and concomitant medicines and took more than seven days to remit. Gaps: (1) causal wording from a non-randomized comparison with a historical cohort, different parent trials, an age difference, unblinded ratings and no adjustment; the authors list most of these limits but the abstract does not; (2) the outcome is withdrawal during fixed morphine substitution, so the finding is that this morphine regimen suppressed withdrawal less well in the fentanyl cohort, as the abstract also says, not a description of untreated fentanyl withdrawal; (3) 'more than seven days to remit' conflicts with the Results, where self-rated scores returned to the earlier cohort's level by day 7, and measurement stopped at day 7; (4) concomitant medicines were available only to the Fentanyl cohort, which would narrow rather than widen the difference in symptoms but complicates the vital-sign comparison; (5) suggestions about short-term opioid bridging and cimetidine go beyond the data.

timeline.event: Dunn et al. trial of extended-release tramadol for opioid withdrawal, the parent trial of the Non-Fentanyl cohort (as cited by this paper).
Luba et al. and Thakrar et al. on fentanyl withdrawal severity, body mass index and urine fentanyl concentration (as cited by this paper; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: A single, small, historically controlled comparison from one research unit. It is consistent with clinical reports that fentanyl withdrawal is harder to control with standard opioid regimens, but no study with a contemporaneous comparison group or adjustment for confounding has confirmed it in the papers read for this card.

funding.funder: National Institutes of Health grants R01DA018125, R01DA048761 and T32DA007209.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit (the first author also at Friends Research Institute, Baltimore); the same group ran both parent trials.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study enrolling people with fentanyl-positive and fentanyl-negative urine at the same time and place, testing all urine by chromatography for fentanyl, xylazine and nitazenes, recording amount and recency of use and body mass index, rating withdrawal blind to exposure, adjusting for age and other drug use, and following withdrawal both under a standard medicine regimen and after it ends.

domains.note: Cohorts about a decade apart from different parent trials with different diagnostic criteria and age limits; the Fentanyl group was five years older; no adjustment; era-related changes in the supply (xylazine, nitazenes) and in the population cannot be separated from fentanyl exposure.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Exposure defined by a single entry urine test; non-fentanyl status confirmed by chromatography in only 3 of 103; amount, recency and co-use (including heroin within the Fentanyl group) not measured.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteers for residential research trials in two eras; the Fentanyl cohort is the first 30 of an ongoing trial; selection into each trial may relate to withdrawal experience.

Concomitant medicines for withdrawal symptoms (including clonazepam, loperamide and trazodone) were available only in the Fentanyl trial, introduced because withdrawal was uncontrolled; they could change symptoms and vital signs differently in the two groups.
The number contributing ratings on each day and any departures during the stabilization week are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-ratings by participants aware of their own drug history; observers not necessarily blind to fentanyl exposure, as the authors state.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Secondary analysis without a registered plan; about 35 outcomes without correction; the abstract and the Results give different day ranges for the group differences.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two domains are high (confounding by era, trial and age with no adjustment; concomitant medicines available to one cohort only), so the overall judgment is high. The direction of the main difference is unlikely to be produced by the concomitant medicines, which would narrow it, but confounding by era and supply could plausibly produce or enlarge it. The paper may be cited as one small historically controlled comparison showing more self-rated and observer-rated withdrawal, and more tachycardia, in a fentanyl-exposed cohort under the same fixed morphine regimen; it should not be cited as showing that fentanyl causes worse withdrawal, for the course of untreated fentanyl withdrawal, or for any effect size.

key_findings.finding: 133 participants: 103 in the Non-Fentanyl cohort (2010 to 2015) and 30 in the Fentanyl cohort (2021 to February 2024); 56% Black or African American, 84% men; the Fentanyl cohort was older (mean 46.0, SD 10.1, against 41.2, SD 10.2; p = 0.021), with no other significant demographic difference.

Peak self-rated withdrawal (SOWS) differed by cohort, day and cohort-by-day (model F(1,6) = 12.44, p < 0.01): the Fentanyl cohort scored higher on stabilization days 2 to 6, with an inverted-U course peaking on day 2 and returning to the earlier cohort's level by day 7, while the Non-Fentanyl cohort declined steadily from day 1.
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Total Peak Scores, 1st paragraph; Figure 1A legend
key_findings.note: The abstract gives days 2 to 5 for the self-rated difference.

key_findings.finding: Severe self-rated withdrawal was more common in the Fentanyl cohort on day 2 (48% against 16%), day 3 (47% against 8%), day 4 (37% against 6%) and day 5 (27% against 6%); mild ratings were less common (for example day 2, 17% against 58%); days 1 and 7 did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Withdrawal Categorical Ratings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: No single symptom drove the difference: anxiety, sweating, tearing, runny nose, goosebumps, shaking, hot and cold flushes, bone and muscle aches, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, twitching and stomach cramps all showed cohort, day and interaction effects; yawning and the urge to use showed only day and interaction effects. For example, mean anxiety (0 to 4) on day 2 was 2.1 (SD 1.3) in the Fentanyl cohort against 0.9 (SD 1.0).
key_findings.locator: Results › Self-Reported Withdrawal (SOWS) › Individual Symptom Ratings, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Peak observer-rated withdrawal (COWS) differed by cohort, day and interaction (F(1,6) = 7.76, p < 0.001), higher in the Fentanyl cohort on days 2 to 7 and peaking on days 2 and 3. No participant reached moderately severe or severe COWS scores; the proportion with mild observer-rated withdrawal was higher in the Fentanyl cohort on days 2 to 7 (for example day 3, 70% against 13%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Observed Withdrawal (COWS) › Total Peak Scores, 1st paragraph; Withdrawal Categorical Ratings, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The abstract gives days 2 to 6 for the observer-rated difference.

key_findings.finding: Tachycardia (heart rate above 100 at least once) occurred in 43% of the Fentanyl cohort against 19% (p < 0.05); heart rate rose more steeply over the week in the Fentanyl cohort (interaction p = 0.007). Diastolic pressure showed a cohort-by-day interaction (p = 0.022). Pupils were smaller in the Fentanyl cohort on every day (cohort effect p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Results › Physiological Measures › Heart Rate, 1st paragraph; Blood Pressure, 1st paragraph; Pupil Diameter, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Concomitant medicines for withdrawal symptoms were made available during stabilization in the Fentanyl trial only, because of a pattern of uncontrolled withdrawal; none were provided in the Non-Fentanyl trial.

The authors list as limitations the decade between cohorts, morphine's possibly poor fit for stabilizing people exposed to fentanyl, incomplete urine confirmation in the earlier cohort, possible xylazine in the local fentanyl supply, observers not necessarily blind to exposure, the small Fentanyl group, and possible other synthetic opioids such as nitazenes.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the groups differed on stabilization days 2 to 5 (self-rated) and 2 to 6 (observer-rated); the Results give days 2 to 6 and days 2 to 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: The duration of the difference is uncertain by a day at each end; the Results text is the more detailed source.

reporting_issues.issue: The same F statistic with one set of degrees of freedom is printed for different model terms with different p values (for heart rate, F(1,6) = 16.12 with p < 0.001 for day, p = 0.007 for the interaction and p = 0.416 for cohort; similarly for blood pressure and pupil diameter), and F(1,6) cannot be the degrees of freedom for a repeated-measures model in 133 people over 7 days.
reporting_issues.consequence: The test statistics appear to be an overall model statistic repeated for each term; only the p values can be used, and they cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: In the diastolic blood-pressure paragraph, a significant cohort effect is attributed to systolic pressure (p = 0.003), although the systolic paragraph reports no cohort effect (p = 0.504); the same paragraph describes the Fentanyl group's diastolic interaction as a steeper increase in heart rate.
reporting_issues.consequence: Copy errors; the cohort effect probably concerns diastolic pressure, but this cannot be confirmed without the supplementary table.

reporting_issues.issue: The SOWS severity categories (mild 1 to 10, moderate 11 to 20, severe 21 to 30) do not cover scores from 31 to 64.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear how scores above 30 were categorized; presumably as severe.

reporting_issues.issue: Tachycardia is defined as heart rate above 100 at least once (Methods) but reported as more than one incidence (Results).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 43% and 19% may use either definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that withdrawal took more than seven days to remit, while the Results report that self-rated scores returned to the earlier cohort's level by day 7, and data collection ended at day 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: Remission after day 7 was not measured; the statement extrapolates beyond the data.
